newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OLYMPICS-CAPE TOWN STILL ON TRACK DESPITE CRIME.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-CAPE TOWN STILL ON TRACK DESPITE CRIME.

text.p: Cape Town officials faced questions about crime and instability in South Africa when they tried to persuade Olympic chiefs to give the city the 2004 Olympics on Thursday but they still looked confident of staying in the bidding race.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) brought up the thorny issues when a Cape Town delegation was among 11 cities who presented their bids to host the Summer Games to an IOC meeting.

The IOC will announce a final shortlist of the best four or five cities on Friday. Cape Town is believed to have a very good chance of being among the candidates who will face a vote at the IOC's session in September when the venue will be decided.

But the city, bidding to take the Games to Africa for the first time, needed to stress that South Africa was winning its fight against crime and the country would remain stable when President Nelson Mandela leaves office in 1999.

"In 1994 we inherited an unacceptable high level of crime and there was a high level of corruption in the police," South African's Speaker of the House Frene Ginwala said. "We have arrested and charged more police in this time than in the 40 years before that."
The bid's executive officer Chris Ball added: "You have to get crime in Cape Town into perspective. Crime at the Olympic Games will not be an issue."
Cape Town has a battle on its hands to match the facilities and organisation of the highly-regarded bids from Rome, Athens, Buenos Aires and Stockholm who are expected to make up the shortlist.
But the city has a very strong political case. It would certainly be a surprise if it failed to make the list.

The delegations from the other four cities were all quietly confident after their meetings with the IOC's selection college. Buenos Aires is looking to take the Games to South America for the first time.
The only problem for the leading quartet will be if the IOC decides to nominate just four cities including Cape Town. Then eithter Stockholm or Athens may be forced out.

Ginwala said Cape Town told the IOC there would be continuity in the country despite the fact Mandela would be handing over control of the African National Congress (ANC) later this year and would not be standing in the 1999 election.
"When any society has men and women of great achievement people ask these questions," she said. "The issue is being addressed...Collective decisions are made in South Africa."

Cape Town stressed it would be representing a whole continent but the delegation, which included Sports Minister Steve Tshwete, was quick to point out it was not just in Lausanne to plead a political case.
"We have not just come for a political award," Ginwala said. "Technically we are on a par with the other bids."

The outsiders -- Istanbul, Lille, Rio de Janeiro, San Juan, Seville and St Petersburg -- were also trying to impress the IOC of their qualities but none of them were expected to pull off a surprise by making the shortlist.
Even before Friday's announcement, Istanbul continued to attack the IOC's system of reducing the candidates without a vote of all its members. Its delegation seemed resigned to losing.
Rio brought Pele to Lausanne to back its bid but one of the world's greatest soccer players and sporting ambassadors looked set to leave Switzerland disappointed.
